Where is Columbia, Missouri, and who owns homes here?

Columbia is the seat of Boone County in central Missouri, about 120 miles from both St. Louis and Kansas City and 29 miles north of Jefferson City. The July 1, 2025 Census Bureau estimate puts Columbia at 130,851 people, up from 108,500 in 2010.

It is the largest of the four Missouri cities in this series, and the only one where fewer than half of homes are owner-occupied. With the university, three hospital systems and state government nearby, many houses in town have spent time as rentals.

Columbia figures from Census QuickFacts, 2020 to 2024 estimates
MeasureColumbia
Home value for owners, median$284,600
Owner-occupied housing rate48.7%
Median gross rent$1,097
Persons per household2.26
Mean commute to work16.4 minutes
Adults with a bachelor's degree or higher56.7%

The city covers 66.54 square miles of land, so the value of a house depends heavily on which side of town it is on and how close it sits to the university.

How did Columbia grow from a creek-side village into a university city?

Settlers from Kentucky and Virginia moved into the Boonslick region in the early 1800s. Boone County was formed in 1820, and the first village, Smithton, struggled because wells hit bedrock. Springs along Flat Branch Creek drew the town across the creek, and Columbia was laid out in the spring of 1821 and named the county seat that year.

The city bid hard for the state university and raised three times what any rival offered. The University of Missouri sits downtown beside Stephens College and Columbia College, and education, medicine and insurance have anchored the economy since.

Hills, creek valleys and the cave systems of Rock Bridge State Park give the terrain a feel closer to the Ozarks than the northern plains. Hinkson, Perche and Flat Branch creeks run through town, so check the flood map for any house near a stream valley.

Which employers, schools and roads shape Columbia house sales?

The University of Missouri tops the 2022 list of city employers with 8,709 people, followed by University of Missouri Health Care at 5,092, Veterans United Home Loans at 3,474 and Columbia Public Schools at 2,650. The Truman Veterans' Hospital, Boone Hospital Center, the City of Columbia and Shelter Insurance also employ more than 1,000 each.

Columbia Public Schools serves almost all of the city, with four high schools: Hickman, Rock Bridge, Muriel Battle and Frederick Douglass. A very small part of the city is in the Hallsville R-IV district.

  • Interstate 70 and US 63 are the main freeways, and Routes 763, 163 (Providence Road) and 740 (Stadium Boulevard) cross the city.
  • The MKT Trail connects across town, and Columbia Regional Airport is the only commercial airport in mid-Missouri.
  • MoDOT's Improve I-70 project plans a third lane in each direction for roughly 200 miles between Blue Springs and Wentzville, with the Columbia to Kingdom City segment expected to take four to five years.

What city offices and programs help Columbia homeowners?

The city's Housing and Neighborhood Services department runs several programs that touch a house sale. Its Office of Neighborhood Services handles code enforcement at 573-817-5050, and the Housing Programs Division at 573-874-6321 runs federal and local housing aid.

  • The Homeownership Assistance Program helps make buying more affordable for eligible buyers.
  • The Home Rehab and Energy Efficiency Program brings existing homes up to property maintenance and rehabilitation standards.
  • The Neighborhood Cleanup Program supports block cleanups.

Census numbers show a mobile population. Only 77.5 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, against 88.0 percent in Blue Springs, and 11.6 percent of Columbia residents are 65 or older.

What is Columbia's weather, and how does it affect a house?

Weather swings sharply here, with a humid continental pattern. The July average is 78.5 degrees, the January average is 31 degrees, and the city sees about 35 days a year at 90 degrees or higher. Snow averages 16.5 inches a season, and spring brings the most severe weather.

Hot summers test air conditioning and attic ventilation, while freezes and storms put the pressure on roofs, gutters and older plumbing. Inspectors will check those first.

What does Columbia's Rental Unit Conservation Law mean for a seller?

Every rental unit in Columbia needs a Certificate of Compliance, and it is unlawful to operate a rental without a current one. A buyer of a former rental will want to know the certificate is valid.

  • Certificates last five years, with an inspection at each renewal.
  • Fees from January 1, 2025 are $130 for a single-family dwelling and $195 for a duplex.
  • A short-term rental unit pays a $130 application and inspection fee.
  • A certificate can be transferred after a sale within 90 days of title transfer for $15, and it carries over for the unexpired part of its term.

Applying involves an HVAC certification for gas appliances, then an inspection. Neighborhood Services at 11 N. Seventh Street, phone 573-817-5050, handles applications and transfers.

How are Boone County property taxes handled when a Columbia house sells?

The Boone County Collector mails tax statements in November, and real estate tax is due upon receipt but no later than December 31. The 2026 statements went out November 4, 2026, and the penalty-free deadline is December 31, 2026.

The collector's page explains that taxes are a lien that stays with the property, and the new owner is liable for unpaid taxes when ownership changes. Taxes are generally prorated between buyer and seller, with the buyer credited at closing for the months the seller owned the house. No money is paid to the collector at the sale itself. If you close on or after October 1, the bill may still be issued in the seller's name, and you should tell the collector the new owner's name and address.

The assessor values a house at 19 percent of its market value for tax purposes. Unpaid taxes can lead to a public tax certificate sale held on the fourth Monday in August. Boone County also has a Senior Real Estate Tax Relief Program for approved primary residences.

Where does a Columbia seller record the deed?

Deeds for Columbia addresses are filed at the Boone County Government Center, 801 East Walnut, Room 132, in Columbia. The phone number is 573-886-4345. The office records real estate documents, including deeds, deeds of trust, releases and easements, and it is the source your title company will use for a clean history of the parcel.

Property boundary maps are updated by the Assessor's office from warranty deeds the recorder receives.

What options does a Columbia seller have to sell fast?

A Columbia owner can hire an agent, go without one, or take an as-is offer from an investor. Houses with tenants in place or a lapsed rental certificate can be harder to sell on the open market, so owners of those properties often look at a direct purchase.

Gather your payoff letter, Boone County tax statement, rental certificate status and school district first. That packet lets you compare a listing's net proceeds against a cash offer without delay.

More questions about Columbia, MO

Does a Columbia rental certificate transfer to the buyer?

Yes. The city allows transfer within 90 days of title transfer for a $15 fee, and the certificate keeps its unexpired term. Call Neighborhood Services at 573-817-5050 to arrange it.

When are Boone County property taxes due?

Upon receipt of the bill, and no later than December 31. For 2026 the last day to pay without penalties and fees is December 31, 2026.

Who pays the property tax at closing?

Taxes are generally prorated, with the buyer credited by the seller for the months the seller owned the house. The collector says no tax money is paid to its office at closing.

Where is the Boone County Recorder of Deeds?

At the Boone County Government Center, 801 East Walnut, Room 132 in Columbia. Call 573-886-4345 with questions about copies or filings.

Which school district serves my Columbia house?

Almost all of the city is in Columbia Public Schools, and a very small part lies in the Hallsville R-IV district. Check the district boundary for your address.

Why do people buy houses in Blue Springs?

Blue Springs is a Jackson County suburb east of Kansas City, and a 2025 Census Bureau estimate puts the population at 61,632. It is the tenth-largest city in Missouri and one of the biggest in the Kansas City metro.

The city covers about 22 square miles and has grown fast since the 1960s. Its population went from 6,779 in 1970 to 25,936 in 1980, then settled into steadier gains of roughly 5 to 12 percent a decade. Most houses here were built in that postwar commuter boom, so a typical seller is dealing with a house that is 20 to 50 years old.

Blue Springs facts from the Census Bureau, QuickFacts, 2020 to 2024 estimates
MeasureBlue Springs
Typical home value for owners$263,100
Owner-occupied housing rate68.9%
Median gross rent$1,277
Households22,908
Mean commute to work25.7 minutes
Median household income$88,920

That 25.7 minute commute is the longest of the four Missouri cities in this series, which fits a place where many owners drive into Kansas City for work.

How did Blue Springs get its name and its shape?

The name comes from a spring on a hillside that feeds a tributary of the Little Blue River. Freighters on the Santa Fe route used it as a stopping point as early as 1825, and settler Franklin Smith arrived from Virginia in 1838 and opened the first post office in 1845.

In March 1878 the Chicago and Alton Railroad announced a station about a mile east, and the town moved its center to follow the tracks. The county court approved incorporation on September 7, 1880. The city became a fourth-class city in 1904 and adopted a home rule charter in April 1994.

For a seller, that history shows up in the map. The old town sits around Main Street downtown, where the city is working through a multi-phase streetscape project, while the large subdivisions spread out along Adams Dairy Parkway and Missouri Route 7.

Which schools, roads and employers affect a Blue Springs house sale?

The Blue Springs R-IV School District covers the vast majority of addresses, and smaller pieces fall in the Lee's Summit R-VII and Grain Valley R-V districts. Buyers with children often start their search by district, so confirm which one your address falls in before you write a listing or describe the house to a cash buyer.

Interstate 70 runs through the city toward Kansas City on one side and Columbia and St. Louis on the other. US 40, Missouri Route 7 and Adams Dairy Parkway handle most local trips. The largest local employers listed in the city's 2022 financial report include the Blue Springs School District with 2,147 employees, Hy-Vee, St. Mary's Hospital of Blue Springs, Faurecia Interiors Systems and Fike Corporation.

  • Fleming Park, with Blue Springs Lake and Lake Jacomo, covers 7,809 acres.
  • Central Jackson County Fire Protection District handles fire and ambulance service for most of the city.
  • Two Mid-Continent Public Library branches serve residents.

What does Blue Springs require before you repair, rent or sell a house?

Building permits come from the Codes Administration Division of Community Development at 903 W. Main Street, phone 816-228-0118. The city moved to the 2024 International Residential and Building Codes on June 1, 2026. Applications filed before that date follow the older codes, and permitted projects keep the code in force when the permit was issued.

Roofs get special attention. A permit is required only when structural roof decking is replaced, but any repair covering more than 10 percent of the roof within three years counts as a full roof covering replacement. Inspection requests must reach the Building Inspection Hotline at 816-228-0104 by 3 p.m. the day before.

The city's top code tips also matter for a house you plan to show:

  • Lawns must stay under 8 inches and noxious plants must be removed.
  • Inoperable vehicles belong inside a garage or off the property.
  • Cars and trucks may not park on grass.
  • Fence, deck and pool work needs a building permit, and that includes any pool that can hold 24 inches of water.

Can a new owner rent a Blue Springs house by the night?

Yes, but only after registering with the city and getting a business license. The business license fee is $50 per business plus $2 per employee, and each license runs out at the end of February.

The registration packet asks for the property address and parcel details, the number of bedrooms, parking, a local responsible agent reachable around the clock, and tax compliance acknowledgments. Operators must follow occupancy limits and quiet hours, and commercial events are prohibited. Hotel and motel tax returns are due by month's end for the previous month. Ask Business Services at 816-228-0131 before you tell a buyer a house can be used this way.

What happens to Jackson County tax bills when a Blue Springs house sells?

Jackson County bills real estate tax each year and the bill is due December 31, using the postmark to decide whether a mailed payment is on time. Interest, penalties and fees apply to anything paid after that date.

The county explains the math this way: houses are assessed at 19 percent of what the assessor thinks they would sell for, and the tax is the taxable value divided by 100 and multiplied by the combined levy rate of the school district, city, fire district and other taxing bodies. Its worked example turns a $110,000 house into a $744.50 bill. Ask the Collection office for the current balance on your parcel before closing so your closing agent can settle the year.

If you think the value is too high, the Board of Equalization hears appeals, and its 2026 filing window ran until July 13, 2026. Documents that support a lower value include a certified appraisal, a sales contract with the settlement statement, and written repair estimates. A real estate agent's opinion of value does not count.

Who files the deed after a Blue Springs sale?

Deeds for Blue Springs addresses are recorded with the Jackson County Recorder of Deeds, and the county lists a recording office at the Historic Truman Courthouse, 112 W. Lexington, Suite 30, Independence (816-881-4483).

Page one of a deed must list the document title, its date, every grantor with marital status, every grantee, any statutory addresses and the legal description, all below the three inch top margin. A title company normally prepares and files the deed for you.

How can a Blue Springs owner sell quickly?

Blue Springs owners have three paths: an agent's listing, a private sale, or a direct purchase by an investor. A listing usually brings the widest pool of buyers, but it also means showings, buyer inspections and repair requests, which matter for a house that needs a roof or has deferred maintenance.

A direct sale gives up some price in return for speed and fewer contingencies. Before you compare offers, collect your mortgage payoff, the latest Jackson County tax bill, any open permits, and the school district for the address. Those four documents answer most of what a buyer or title company will ask in the first week.

More questions about Blue Springs, MO

Which county do I deal with when I sell in Blue Springs?

Jackson County handles the deed, the tax bill and the assessment for a Blue Springs address. The city itself issues building permits and business licenses, so you will work with both offices.

What is the property tax deadline on a Blue Springs house?

December 31 each year, based on the postmark for mailed payments. The county adds interest, penalties and fees to anything paid after that date, so find out from your closing agent how this year's bill will be split.

Can I still appeal my Jackson County assessment for 2026?

No, the 2026 Board of Equalization window ended July 13, 2026. Contact the Assessment office about the next value notice and keep an appraisal or sale paperwork ready for the next filing window.

Is a permit required for a new roof in Blue Springs?

Only when structural roof decking is replaced, according to the Codes Administration Division. Repairs over 10 percent of the roof area in a three year span are treated as a full roof covering replacement under the updated code.

Does Blue Springs allow short-term rentals?

Yes, with city registration and a business license. The operator needs a local responsible agent, must respect occupancy and quiet hour limits, and files monthly lodging tax returns. Call Business Services at 816-228-0131 for the packet.

What is Chesterfield like, and what do houses cost here?

Chesterfield is a western suburb of St. Louis in St. Louis County, about 25 miles from downtown, and the Census Bureau counted an estimated 49,309 people on July 1, 2025. It incorporated in 1988 and was the state's 14th largest city at the 2020 census.

It is the priciest of the four Missouri cities in this series, and its population slipped 1.4 percent from the April 2020 estimates base. Owners here are older and have higher incomes than in the other three cities, which shapes who looks at a house for sale.

One resident in four is past 65, so many Chesterfield sellers are downsizing or settling an estate rather than relocating for work.

The city covers 31.88 square miles of land, with 2.35 people per household, and retail sales of about $30,747 per resident in 2022. Median monthly owner costs run $2,464 with a mortgage and $946 without one, which tells you what a buyer will weigh against your asking price.

How did Chesterfield come together as a city?

Chesterfield was built from several small communities. Bellefontaine, nicknamed Hilltown, dates to about 1837. Lake began as Hog Hollow around 1850, Gumbo grew in the river valley at what is now Chesterfield Airport Road and Long Road, and Monarch sprang up along the Rock Island rail line in the late 1870s.

The valley was once called Gumbo Flats because the silty soil turns to mud when wet. A violent F4 tornado crossed St. Louis County on January 24, 1967, and the area was submerged in the Great Flood of 1993. Higher levees followed, and the valley is now commercial, with Spirit of St. Louis Airport and a long outdoor strip of stores.

The practical point for sellers is that parts of the city sit in the Missouri River floodplain. Ask your lender or title company whether your parcel needs flood insurance.

Who lives in Chesterfield, and what do they ask of a house?

Census figures show a settled, well-connected community. About 86.8 percent of people had not moved in the past year, 96.5 percent of households have broadband, and poverty sits at 3.9 percent.

  • Foreign-born residents make up 16.0 percent of the population, and 16.1 percent speak a language other than English at home.
  • Asian residents are 13.2 percent of the city, the highest share among the four Missouri cities in this series.
  • Veterans number 2,141.

Education is a draw. Logan University offers chiropractic and rehabilitation programs in the city, and Chesterfield Montessori School, Ascension School and Incarnate Word School serve younger children alongside the public districts. Barat Academy, a private high school, closed in 2025.

Which schools, employers and roads matter to a Chesterfield buyer?

Two districts serve the city. Rockwood School District covers the western part and Parkway School District covers the east, and schools inside the city include Parkway Central, Parkway West and Marquette high schools. Buyers often ask the district first, so put it in your notes.

The city's 2013 financial report named St. Luke's Hospital (3,447 employees), Parkway School District, Bayer, Delmar Gardens and Reinsurance Group of America among its largest employers. Dierbergs, Amdocs and MOHELA appear on the same list.

  • Interstate 64, called Highway 40 locally, has seven exits in the city.
  • Missouri Route 340, or Olive Boulevard, runs east and west through town, and Route 141 forms the eastern edge with Town and Country.
  • Faust Park, with the Butterfly House and a carousel, and the Chesterfield Amphitheater are the best known recreation sites.

Do you need a city permit to repair or sell a Chesterfield house?

Repairs and additions go through the city's Planning Department. Its page describes a building permit as the way to confirm a project is structurally sound and meets building and zoning codes. Call the department before work on structure, additions or exterior changes.

The city's occupancy permit requirement is written for businesses: a permit or re-occupancy permit applies to every new business and every change of business use, tenancy or ownership. If you own a commercial space or a mixed property, that rule matters to your buyer. For an ordinary house sale, ask Chesterfield's Planning Department whether any permit applies to your address.

The city says its occupancy approvals check compliance with city, county and fire district codes, so expect more than one office to be involved. Close any open permit before you list.

How do St. Louis County property taxes work for a Chesterfield seller?

The St. Louis County Assessor values every parcel, and state law section 137.115 requires reassessment as of January 1 of each odd-numbered year. The assessor does not run the appeals board, which is independent. Appeals must be filed or postmarked by the second Monday in July, and the 2026 date was July 13, 2026, which has passed.

The Collector of Revenue bills property tax, and it must be paid or postmarked by December 31 of the billed year. Payments made after that date are subject to up to 18 percent annual interest plus a 2 percent penalty under Missouri law, according to the collector's delinquent tax page.

Property tax is a lien on the house, so expect the closing agent to confirm the current year. Ask the collector's office for the exact balance on your parcel.

Where is a Chesterfield deed recorded, and what does it cost?

Deeds for Chesterfield are recorded with the St. Louis County Recorder of Deeds, 41 S. Central Avenue, Clayton, MO 63105. You can mail or drop off the original notarized document with a check or money order made out to ROD, or use an approved eRecording vendor.

The county charges $26 on page one and $3 on every page after it, and adds $25 when a document ignores the state's formatting standards. The original comes back within about a week of recording. Most owners leave this step to the title company.

What are your choices for selling a Chesterfield house quickly?

Because values are high and buyers are choosy, a Chesterfield house in good condition can attract the open market and sell on an agent's listing. A house that needs a kitchen, roof or systems work, or one tied up in an estate, may do better with a direct as-is purchase where the buyer handles repairs.

Get your payoff letter, county tax statement, school district and any permit history together first. With those in hand, you can compare an agent's net proceeds with a cash offer on equal terms.

St. Louis County, through the Recorder of Deeds at 41 S. Central Avenue in Clayton. A deed costs $26 for the first page and $3 for each extra page.

When are St. Louis County property taxes due?

December 31 of the billed year, with the postmark counting for mailed payments. Later payments accrue up to 18 percent yearly interest plus a 2 percent penalty.

Can I still appeal my St. Louis County value this year?

No. The 2026 deadline was July 13, 2026, the second Monday in July. Ask the Equalization board when the next filing window opens.

Which school district is my Chesterfield house in?

Rockwood School District serves the west side of the city and Parkway School District serves the east. Confirm the district for your address with the school district's boundary tools before listing.

Does Chesterfield's occupancy permit apply when I sell my home?

The city's occupancy permit page is aimed at businesses, covering new businesses and changes of use, tenancy or ownership. Call the Planning Department to confirm for your address.

Where is Cape Girardeau, and what is the housing market like?

Cape Girardeau sits on the west bank of the Mississippi River in Southeast Missouri, between St. Louis and Memphis along Interstate 55. The Census Bureau's July 1, 2025 estimate is 40,977 people, spread over about 29 square miles of land.

The housing numbers here run well below the other big Missouri cities. Homes are valued lower, more households rent, and a university and two large hospitals shape who is buying and moving.

Cape Girardeau figures from Census QuickFacts, 2020 to 2024 estimates
MeasureCape Girardeau
Middle home value among owners$196,300
Owner-occupied housing rate54.0%

Residents age 65 and over19.7%

With barely more than half of homes owner-occupied, a Cape Girardeau house that has been a rental is not unusual.

How did the river and the railroad shape Cape Girardeau?

A French trader named Jean Pierre Girardeau set up a post on a rocky bluff in the early 1760s, and the city takes its name from that cape. Louis Lorimier founded the community on January 4, 1793, under a Spanish land grant. The town was platted in 1806, incorporated in 1808 and made a city by the legislature in 1843.

Steamboats made it the largest port on the Mississippi between St. Louis and Memphis. The first railroad arrived in the early 1880s, and the city's population more than doubled between 1900 and 1920. The International Shoe Company factory built in 1907 gave the Red Star neighborhood its name, because many workers lived nearby.

Floods from the Mississippi hit the riverfront repeatedly between 1927 and 1951. The Army Corps of Engineers finished a floodwall and levee of more than a mile in 1964, and the city now owns and maintains it. The city's online maps include a flood zone layer, which is the place to check a parcel near the river.

Which employers and schools drive demand for Cape Girardeau houses?

Health care leads. St. Francis Medical Center employs about 3,143 people and Mercy Hospital Southeast about 2,950. Procter & Gamble, Southeast Missouri State University, Cape Girardeau Public Schools, Drury Hotels and Century Casino complete the list of large local employers.

The city is mostly in the Cape Girardeau Public Schools district, with a section of Cape Girardeau County in the Jackson R-II district. A small part of the city lies in Scott County, where Scott City R-I covers most of that area. Check your parcel before you tell a buyer which district applies.

  • Southeast Missouri State University has a main campus and a River Campus in the city.
  • The Cape Girardeau Regional Airport opened a new passenger terminal in 2024.
  • Local roads include Interstate 55, Kingshighway and the Bill Emerson Memorial Bridge, which opened in 2003.

What does the Cape Girardeau climate mean for a house?

Cape Girardeau sits in the humid subtropical zone. Average yearly precipitation is about 47.9 inches, spring is the wettest season, and the record high is 107 degrees on June 29, 2012. The airport sees about 47 days a year at 90 degrees or hotter.

That means air conditioning, attic ventilation, roof condition and basement dampness draw the most attention in a buyer inspection. Winters bring a mix of rain, sleet and snow, with about 12.8 days a year that never rise above freezing.

What rules does Cape Girardeau have for rental houses and repairs?

The city licenses residential rentals and enforces a checklist of safety and condition standards through Inspection Services at City Hall, 44 N. Lorimier Street, phone 573-339-6327. Standards include working smoke alarms in every bedroom, in the hallway outside bedrooms and on each floor, bedroom egress windows with a clear opening of at least 24 inches high and 30 inches wide, handrails on steps with four or more risers, and guards on landings more than 30 inches high.

With tenants in the house, ask the department whether the license is current, because a buyer investor will want that answer.

For repair work, inspection requests received after 11:30 a.m. are scheduled for the next day, final inspections need 24 hours notice, and approved plans must be on site. The city became a Certified Local Government in 1991 and its Historic Preservation Commission reviews Certificate of Appropriateness applications in local historic districts. Ask the planning division whether your street is in one before you plan exterior changes.

What local details should a Cape Girardeau seller know?

Cape Girardeau became a constitutional home rule city in 1982 with a council-manager form of government, and voters adopted ward representation in 1993. City Hall moved to 44 N. Lorimier Street in 2022, where the Common Pleas Courthouse and the Carnegie Library were joined into one building.

  • A half-percent local sales tax pays for the city's Transportation Trust Fund, which funds street work.
  • Old Town Cape, the downtown Main Street group, has worked on revitalization since 1999.
  • Cape Rock Park marks the remains of the bluff that gave the city its name.
  • Census data put the share of residents below the poverty line at 20.8 percent, and 17.4 percent of residents are under 18.

How do Cape Girardeau County assessments and taxes work?

The county assessor, whose office is at 1 Barton Square, Suite 201 in Jackson, values every parcel. State law requires reassessment of existing real property as of January 1 of each odd-numbered year, and new improvements are added when construction finishes.

Tax rates come from the school, library, fire and other districts, not from the assessor. The assessor's website has a real estate search and parcel map, and the office handles the Missouri Property Tax Credit form 948 for qualifying seniors and disabled owners. Call 573-243-2468 or email appraisal@capecounty.us for value questions.

Ask the Cape Girardeau County Collector for your current bill, and ask your closing agent how the year gets divided.

How is a deed recorded in Cape Girardeau County?

Deeds go to the county Recorder of Deeds at #1 Barton Square, Suite 203, Jackson, phone 573-243-8123, with weekday hours of 8:00 to 4:30. Documents can be mailed, dropped off or e-recorded.

The recording fee for a standard document is $24 on page one plus $3 per added page, and a document that misses the formatting standards carries an extra $25. Pages must be 8.5 by 11 inches, with a three inch margin on the first page left blank for the recorder's stamp. The office cannot create documents or give legal advice, so an attorney or title agent drafts the deed.

What are the ways to sell a Cape Girardeau house fast?

Cape Girardeau owners can hire an agent, go it alone, or ask investors for direct offers. In a market with many renters and a lower price range, houses that need work or carry tenants can sit on the market, so some owners prefer a quick as-is sale.

Whichever route you choose, gather the rental license status, the county tax bill, the mortgage payoff and the school district for the address first. Those items settle most of the questions that come up between a signed contract and closing day.

More questions about Cape Girardeau, MO

Is Cape Girardeau in one county?

Mostly it is in Cape Girardeau County, but a small part of the city lies in Scott County. Check the parcel's county before calling an assessor or recorder.

Where does a Cape Girardeau deed get filed?

The Cape Girardeau County Recorder of Deeds in Jackson, at #1 Barton Square, Suite 203. A standard deed costs $24 on page one plus $3 per extra page, plus $25 if formatting rules are not met.

How often does the county reassess my house?

State law requires reassessment as of January 1 of every odd-numbered year. The assessor also adds new improvements as construction finishes, so a remodel can change the value in any year.

Does my rental house need a license before I sell it?

The city requires residential rental licensing and inspects against a safety checklist. Call Inspection Services at 573-339-6327 to confirm your unit's status, since buyers who plan to keep tenants will ask.

What flood concerns affect Cape Girardeau homes?

Houses near the Mississippi River depend on the floodwall and levee built in 1964. The city publishes interactive maps with flood zone layers, so check your parcel there.

Owners with an unpermitted basement, postponed repairs, an inherited property, tenants or a hard move date often weigh a cash buyer instead. Every route runs into the inspection and tax paperwork covered below, so collect it before you choose.

What is Ballwin like, and who buys homes there?

Ballwin is a western suburb of St. Louis in St. Louis County, with a Government Center at 1 Government Ctr in Vlasis Park. The place dates to 1837 and carries the name of John Ball, who settled the town site in 1804. It incorporated on December 29, 1950, and spreads over roughly 8.98 square miles at an elevation of 623 feet.

Growth came in bursts. Residents numbered 5,710 in 1960, 10,656 in 1970 and 21,816 in 1990, and 31,283 by 2000, after which the count flattened. The 2020 census recorded 31,103 and the 2025 estimate stands at 30,901. In 2020 the median resident was 41.9 years old, 59.7 percent of households were married couples and about a third included children.

School districts come up in nearly every showing. The city is split between the Parkway and Rockwood districts. Parkway West High School, Claymont, Henry, Oak Brook and Sorrento Springs elementary schools are in Ballwin on the Parkway side. Selvidge Middle, Ballwin, Westridge and Woerther elementary schools represent Rockwood. Holy Infant School is a private Catholic school for pre-K through eighth grade. Confirm which district serves your address and say so in the listing or offer conversation.

What do Ballwin homes cost to own?

Federal survey data for 2020 to 2024 describe a high-value city of owners. Roughly 84 percent of homes are lived in by their owners, and the midpoint value of those homes is $377,100.

Does Ballwin require an inspection before I sell?

Yes. Under the city's rule, any occupied building has to be inspected and certified against the Ballwin Housing Code before a new resident, tenant or business moves in, and that occupant needs an Occupancy Permit. The city's MyGov portal handles applications and permits.

Call Building Inspections at 636-227-2129 with questions. The check can be more than a walkthrough. The city's permit page singles out basements: a finish done without permits must be permitted and approved before the house is sold, which can mean opening walls so inspectors see the work.

  • Check for work you or a prior owner did without a permit, such as a basement finish, deck or addition.
  • Fix safety items that a housing code inspector would flag before you schedule.
  • Apply through MyGov and call City Hall to schedule the visit during business hours.
  • Give the buyer or their agent a copy of the passed certificate for closing.

Ballwin adopted the 2024 International codes, including the Property Maintenance Code, in September 2026, replacing the 2015 standards. Ask the department which edition applies to the inspection you are scheduling.

What local features come up when selling in Ballwin?

Parks and the Manchester Road corridor define the city. Vlasis Park, the largest, covers 31 acres north of Manchester Road and hosts the annual Ballwin Days festival. Other city parks include New Ballwin Park, Ferris Park, Greenfield Commons and Holloway Park. The Pointe at Ballwin Commons has an indoor pool and fitness center, the North Pointe Aquatic Center is an outdoor summer pool, and the Ballwin Golf Course sits beside it.

The Bacon Log Cabin museum covers local history, and Lion's Choice, the roast beef chain, started in Ballwin. The city lists a Manchester Road Great Streets Master Plan, and its Planning and Zoning Commission meets at 7 p.m. in the Government Center board room, a useful place to ask about nearby projects.

How do property taxes work for a Ballwin seller?

St. Louis County bills Ballwin houses. The Collector of Revenue wants payment made or postmarked by December 31, and later payments add interest of up to 18 percent a year and a 2 percent penalty.

State law drives the valuation. RSMo 137.115 puts houses at 19 percent of true value, with fresh numbers every odd year, which makes 2027 a reassessment year here. Owners who disagree file with the St. Louis County Board of Equalization, and the 2026 window ran from May 1 to July 13. That date has passed, and the next window opens in the spring of 2027. A later appeal goes to the State Tax Commission by September 30 or thirty days after the board acts, whichever falls later.

The title company usually divides the year's tax between the two sides at the table. Before listing, ask the St. Louis County Collector what is owed and pay off any back year so it does not hold up the sale.

What papers should a Ballwin seller gather first?

Collect the items a buyer, lender and title company will each ask for, and the closing moves with fewer calls back and forth.

  • The Occupancy Permit, or the MyGov application showing the inspection is scheduled.
  • Permits and final approvals for any addition, deck, fence, pool or basement finish.
  • A St. Louis County tax statement for the current year and proof that earlier years are paid.
  • A copy of your recorded deed, which the Recorder of Deeds in Clayton can supply.
  • The names of your school district and any homeowner association, if one applies.

The Government Center at 1 Government Ctr is open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., and permits, inspections and code enforcement are handled there.

How is the deed recorded after a Ballwin sale?

After closing, the deed is filed with the St. Louis County Recorder of Deeds, 41 S. Central Ave, Clayton, MO 63105. Posted charges run $26 for page one and $3 for every later page, with a $25 surcharge for a document that misses Missouri's formatting standards. Electronic filing through a vendor can add that vendor's fee.

The office accepts the notarized original by mail or lobby drop-off, with payment by check or money order, and answers at 314-615-7100. A deed that is never recorded is valid only between the parties and people with actual notice under RSMo 442.400, so make sure the closing agent files it. Most Ballwin sellers rely on the title company for this step.

A house that needs repairs before a typical buyer will close, or one tied up in an estate or a lease, may move faster through a cash purchase, although inspection, tax and recording still apply.

More questions about Ballwin, MO

Yes. Ballwin certifies a building against its Housing Code before a new resident, tenant or business occupies it. Apply in MyGov or phone Inspections at 636-227-2129.

What if my Ballwin basement was finished without a permit?

The city says the house needs a building permit and approval first, and some demolition may be required so the inspector can see the work. Applying before you list saves time.

When are Ballwin property taxes due?

They must be paid or postmarked by December 31. After that, St. Louis County adds interest up to 18 percent a year and a 2 percent penalty.

What will a St. Louis County deed filing run me?

$26 for the opening page and $3 for each page after it, plus $25 when the document is non-standard. The Recorder of Deeds sits in Clayton at 41 S. Central Ave.

What do homes in Ballwin typically sell for by value?

The federal 2020 to 2024 survey puts the midpoint owner-occupied value at $377,100. The city's estimated population on July 1, 2025 was 30,901.

What slows down or speeds up a Belton house sale?

Belton owners can list with an agent, sell without one or take a cash offer, and condition and tenancy usually decide which. The city's rental program, plus Cass County's role in tax and recording, shape the calendar, so line those pieces up early.

Rental houses catch people off guard. Since January 1, 2025, each rental unit inside the city limits must be registered, and the city inspects between tenants. A landlord selling, or a buyer who plans to lease the place out, should read that program before setting a closing date.

Where is Belton, and who lives there?

Belton is a city in northwestern Cass County that belongs to the Kansas City metro area. It sits four miles from the Kansas border on Missouri Route 58, west of I-49 and U.S. 71. Raymore is four miles east, Peculiar is seven miles southeast and Grandview, in Jackson County, is five miles north. The city covers 14.25 square miles of land at about 1,099 feet in elevation.

Belton was platted in 1871 and probably took its name from surveyor Capt. Marcus Lindsey Belt, and its post office has run since 1872. Growth came after World War II. The census counted 1,233 residents in 1950, 4,897 in 1960 and 12,270 in 1970, and the 2020 count was 23,953. Its July 1, 2025 estimate is 26,193. The 2020 median age was 36.1, and 7.7 percent of the 9,936 housing units stood empty.

Belton School District #124 serves most of town with six elementary schools, two middle schools and Belton High School, while part of eastern Belton belongs to the Raymore-Peculiar district. Metropolitan Community College levies tax in the Belton district, and the Cass County Public Library has a branch here.

What do Belton homes and rents look like?

Renters make up a large share of Belton, which helps explain the city's rental program. Survey estimates for 2020 to 2024 show owners in 59 percent of homes, with a midpoint value of $203,200.

What are Belton's rental registration and code enforcement rules?

All rental units inside Belton must be registered, and inspections happen between tenants, after one leaves and before the next moves in. The program took effect on January 1, 2025, under an ordinance the council approved on October 10, 2023.

  • Registration costs $20 per unit and renews every 12 months.
  • A $50 late fee applies to each 30-day period a registration is past due.
  • An inspection done after the tenant has already moved in costs $20.
  • Reinspection fees begin after two failed inspections and are $20 each.

Write to rental@belton.org to book an inspection or ask about the program. Neighborhood Improvement and Code Enforcement, a division of Community Development, enforces the property maintenance and use ordinances. Since October 28, 2024, active violations show on the city's eTRAKiT portal, where a public account lets you view them, apply for permits and schedule inspections. Look up your own address there before you take an offer.

Can I run a short-term rental in Belton?

Only with city approval, and the rules are tight. The council passed Ordinance 2025-4950 on November 25, 2025, and each short-term rental now needs a registration plus a special use permit. The staff report lists a $70 annual registration fee, a $50 inspection fee and a $150 permit fee, at least $270 to begin.

Occupancy is capped at two adults per bedroom plus one more adult per dwelling, with ten guests the ceiling, children included. Hosts remit the city's 5 percent hotel and motel tax monthly, and nobody may register more than five units. The staff report described sites limited to the Old Town Belton area and parcels over three acres, so ask Community Development how the location rule applies to your address.

A temporary carve-out for the 2026 FIFA World Cup covered only June 1 through July 31, 2026, and it expired on August 1, 2026. Operating outside the rules draws fines of $200 to $500, and every day can count as its own offense. A buyer who wants a Belton short-term rental should get the city's answer before closing.

How do Cass County taxes work when I sell in Belton?

Cass County bills real estate once a year, in November, and expects payment on receipt and by December 31, judged by U.S. postmark. Penalties and fees can climb to 25 percent in the first delinquent year. Houses are assessed at 19 percent of market value, and the levy rate is applied per hundred dollars of that assessed figure.

The county's guide for buyers and sellers tells the new owner to pay the full bill by December 31, notes that taxes are generally prorated between the parties and says nothing is paid to the Collector at the sale itself. Because the tax is a lien that stays with the property, a buyer inherits any unpaid amount. Parcels with unpaid tax can go to the annual tax certificate sale, held the fourth Monday of August at the Harrisonville courthouse.

If a bill still arrives in your name after you sell, give the Collector the new owner's name and address. Chris Molendorp is the Collector, at 2725 Cantrell Road in Harrisonville, 816-380-8377, and the Assessor is next door at 2733 Cantrell Road, 816-380-8400.

What should a Belton seller line up before listing?

A short checklist keeps surprises out of the contract period. Belton's own portals and the county offices hold most of what you need.

  • Rental registration and inspection results, if the house has been leased.
  • A look at the eTRAKiT portal for open code violations or permits on the address.
  • The Cass County tax statement and parcel number from the Collector or Assessor.
  • A copy of your deed from the Recorder, plus any release for a paid-off loan.
  • The school district for the address, since eastern Belton can fall in Raymore-Peculiar.

Belton's Old Town area hosts community events through the year, and the city's own planning documents describe it as a mixed-use district of small businesses beside homes. Route 58 and the I-49 and U.S. 71 corridor are the main roads through the area.

Where is the deed recorded after a Belton sale?

Deeds are filed with the Cass County Recorder of Deeds at 102 E. Wall Street in Harrisonville, phone 816-380-8118, open weekdays 8 a.m. until 4 p.m. The office cannot prepare documents for you, so use a title company or a real estate attorney.

The county also offers a fraud alert at casscounty.com/fraud that notifies you when something is recorded under your name. Under RSMo 442.400 an unrecorded deed binds only the parties and anyone with actual notice, so closing agents file right away. A Belton owner short on time because of repairs, tenants, an inherited house or back taxes may find a cash purchase shortens the schedule, with inspection, tax and recording steps unchanged.

More questions about Belton, MO

Does a Belton landlord have to register before selling?

Yes, every rental unit inside Belton must be registered, at $20 per unit a year. Inspections happen between tenants, so a vacated rental should pass before the next occupant or buyer moves in.

Is a short-term rental allowed at a Belton house?

Only with registration and a special use permit under Ordinance 2025-4950. The staff report puts the minimum startup cost at $270, and hosts owe the 5 percent hotel and motel tax.

What is the Cass County tax deadline for a Belton house?

Pay on receipt and by December 31. Late payment can bring penalties and fees as high as 25 percent in the first delinquent year.

Who handles the tax bill at a Belton closing?

Cass County says taxes are generally prorated between buyer and seller and no money goes to the Collector at the sale. The new owner pays the whole bill by December 31.

The 2020 census counted 23,953 and the July 1, 2025 estimate is 26,193. Belton sits in northwestern Cass County within the Kansas City metro area.
